articles.title: We View Consumer Data as Toxic Waste
articles.author: Abhishek Prakash
articles.content:
The VPN industry runs on a promise. Pick almost any provider and the pitch is the same: "we don't keep logs." You hand over your entire internet connection and, in return, you get a pinky-promise that nobody is writing anything down.
For a lot of privacy-minded people, that promise stopped being good enough a while ago. A no-logs policy is only as honest as the company making it, and even an honest company can be hacked, subpoenaed, or quietly acquired.
Obscura VPN is trying to answer to that problem. Instead of asking you to trust its word, it splits the job across two independent companies so that neither one can tie your identity to your browsing. The first hop is Obscura's own servers; the exit hop is run by Mullvad. a respected VPM company out of Sweden. Your traffic is end-to-end encrypted to Mullvad's keys, so Obscura literally can't read it, and Mullvad never sees who you are.
The person behind it is Carl Dong, a former top-5 Bitcoin Core contributor who signs off his own website as "head-janitor" and "I fight for the users." I sent him a set of questions around Obscura. Here's the conversation.
You went from being a top contributor to Bitcoin Core to founding a VPN company. What convinced you the VPN space needed rebuilding rather than just improving?
"Don't Trust, Verify" is a cornerstone of the cypherpunk principles I grew up with. I see this Trust Minimization as crucial when building human-centric, security- and privacy-critical technologies. Yet the VPN industry is riddled with scandals (e.g., Onavo), broken promises, and "no-log" pinky promises. This never sat right with me.
When I saw what Apple's iCloud Private Relay was doing under the hood, I saw what the next generation of VPNs would look like: VPNs that are verifiably private and that outsmart internet censorship. I wanted to make this a reality outside of Apple's walled garden. The world doesn't need another VPN company; it needs a totally new approach to privacy.
Your whole pitch takes direct aim at the "no-logs" model everyone else uses. Why has that promise become inadequate?
The VPN industry is living in the past. Three conglomerates dominate and give the illusion of choice, while betraying their users' trust and operating a payola scheme using media cut-outs to push their talking points. The no-logs pinky-promise has never been adequate for software that can access the entirety of your internet traffic, and verges on being useless in 2026 when LLM-driven cyberattacks run rampant.
At the end of the day, even honest VPN providers who abide by their no-logs policy can be hacked. Users are waking up to this, and there's been an increasing call within the cybersecurity community to stop using VPNs altogether. Obscura is a direct answer to this: you no longer have to trust any single company's word for your internet privacy. That's the way it should have always been.
Walk our readers through the two-party relay in plain terms. How does it actually change the trust model compared to a normal multi-hop VPN?
When you use a traditional VPN, a single company sees your identity (via your connecting IP + your payment information) and your internet traffic. Using a multi-hop option doesn't change the fact that it's still a single company, and oftentimes just adds additional latency for no good reason.
With Obscura's Two-Party Relay, we use a fully independent company (Mullvad) as our second exit hop, with Obscura as the first hop. All of your internet traffic is encrypted to a key controlled by Mullvad's servers, and only relayed through Obscura's servers. That way, Obscura's relay servers never see your actual internet traffic, and Mullvad's exit servers never see your identity (connecting IP or payment information).
For those familiar with Tor, it's like if Tor only had 2 hops, but the hops were dedicated, high-performance hops optimized for maximum speed and reliability.
A skeptic could say you've just moved the trust problem around. Now users trust two companies instead of one, and the two of you could collude or be compelled together. How do you respond?
I'd first lightheartedly point out that using traditional VPNs is just moving trust from your (possibly regulated) ISP to a single wholly unregulated private company. 😆
In all seriousness though, our goal with Obscura is to make sure there's no single party that can jeopardize your internet privacy. No one entity should have that power. With Obscura, as long as either Obscura or Mullvad isn't compromised, no one can correlate your personal identity with your internet activity. This is strictly better than trusting either your ISP or a traditional VPN's pinky-promise.
Let's get technical. Your stealth protocol is built on QUIC to mimic HTTP/3 traffic. Why QUIC specifically, and how does it hold up against serious censorship?
We chose QUIC not only because it looks like HTTP/3, but also because its Unreliable Datagram extension allows us to avoid the TCP-over-TCP meltdown problem that plagues TCP-based VPNs. I'd encourage folks to read this for more details.
As for outsmarting censorship, QUIC has been notably harder for middleboxes to do Deep Packet Inspection on. QUIC allows messages to be fragmented and shuffled across UDP datagrams, which means censorship systems have to reassemble them, making it far more costly. I don't know of any QUIC censorship system currently deployed that does reassembly. More information can be found here.
You accept Monero and Bitcoin over Lightning, need no email, and log in with just a random account number. But Obscura still sees the user's connecting IP. How anonymous can a user really be, and where's the honest limit?
We view consumer data as toxic waste. We don't want it, don't need it, and do as much as possible to make sure you don't have to give us any. Aside from what you mentioned, our website is also accessible over Tor.
But you're absolutely right. We can still see the user's connecting IP address. That will not change unless humanity completely rethinks the OSI stack, which will make the IPv6 transition look like a walk in the park. 😆
The fact that we can't avoid seeing your connecting IP address is the point of Obscura though: if we have to see it, then the most private thing to do is to completely decouple that information from your internet traffic. That's what our Two-Party Relay does.
You've open-sourced the client and talk a lot about reproducible builds, clearly something you carried over from Bitcoin Core. For a non-developer, why do reproducible builds matter for a VPN?
I did a lot of reproducible builds work for Bitcoin Core, so this is near and dear to my heart. I believe that reproducible builds matter for any piece of open-source security-critical software. Even if the published source code is not malicious, that says nothing about the app you download. It essentially answers this question: does the app that I download correspond to the source code that is on GitHub (or whatever other forge you may use).
For Bitcoin Core, a malicious app could mean loss/theft of funds. For VPNs, a malicious app has access to the entirety of your internet traffic and can leak that regardless of the security of your VPN provider.
At Obscura, we of course take reproducible builds seriously. We already have a prototype for Android reproducible builds, and are looking to make other platforms work as well.
Obscura is $8/month, and reviewers note that stacking two providers can cost more than one. Beyond the privacy story, how do you make the economics work as a small team without VC pressure to monetize users?
First, we have no user data to monetize. Second, I think in the tech world we've vastly overcomplicated our businesses. For a business to work, you need your costs to be lower than your revenue over time. That's it. We aren't going to construct a massive data center. We aren't going to put tens of millions into R&D in a lab in Switzerland. We're a small group of six people, working remotely, charging fair prices. As long as we keep our customers happy, we don't have anything to worry about. My goal was never to compare yachts with Bezos.
There's a classic tension between maximum privacy and everyday usability, with Tor as the usual cautionary tale. Where do you draw that line?
The goal is for my mom to use Obscura, and she does! (Hopefully not just because I'm her son.)
I don't think that tension between privacy and usability is always inherent: a VPN doesn't have to be complicated. You should flip a switch and it should just work and you should forget you have it on. The goal is to be seamless. Power users and technical folks who want more should always have the ability to tinker, and we offer that, but the goal is to build a product so good that both feel right at home.
Oftentimes we've also found that giving users a choice is the way to go: while cryptocurrencies may be the most private way to pay for Obscura, my mom is likely to want a credit card option. 😄
Looking at the next few years, with encryption under legislative pressure and tracking everywhere, what worries you most about online privacy?
Every day there is another story about a country or international body proposing new rules that jeopardize the open and free internet we all love. Sometimes these are well-meaning protections that legislators don't fully grasp the ramifications of; other times their motivations are less noble.
What all these scenarios have in common is that, somewhere along the way, behavior that was once considered odd and Orwellian became normalized. You go grab a coffee and you give them your phone number, then you download an app (and allow location permissions), and before you know it companies know every aspect of your life.
Then when you read about how the government can legally purchase this data from data brokers, you start to appreciate just how much of your life can be reconstructed to where you essentially have given away every aspect of your privacy for a free coffee on your birthday. (I'm as guilty as anyone.) So what really worries me is our own complicity in trading privacy for convenience. And I hope with Obscura and other smaller privacy-focused start-ups we can make an easier, simpler to use tech that helps protect people and allows them to make better privacy decisions where there is no trade-off between convenience and privacy.
Finally, a fun one. Your site has a "Cursed Knowledge" page. What's the most cursed thing you've learned about how the internet actually works since starting Obscura?
I think the TLS SNI extension has gotta be one of the most cursed things about how the internet works.
Most people assume that if a connection is encrypted by TLS, then it's fully encrypted. What they don't know is that there's a part of every TLS connection called the SNI where the server's domain name is in plaintext, completely unencrypted! In fact, ISPs and middleboxes often use this as a way to enact internet censorship, since it's a much more reliable mechanism than trying to match connections with DNS requests.
Last year, Obscura was erroneously blocked by a few US ISPs, and SNI was exactly what they used. Of course, using a VPN protects you against that, but it's still quite cursed that TLS has this at all. Hopefully Encrypted Client Hello gets adopted soon so that we can have actual secure TLS!
Whether Obscura's split-trust model is right for you is up to you to decide, but it's definitely a different approach to a problem the VPN world has glossed over for years. The client is open source, so you don't have to take any of this on faith. You can read the code, check your exit hop's key against Mullvad's published list, and verify the claims yourself.
You can learn more at obscura.com, and the source is up on GitHub.
articles.summary:
Obscura VPN introduces a two-party relay system that splits traffic between its own servers and Mullvad to eliminate the need for users to trust a single provider's privacy policy.

### Key Points
- Obscura uses a two-hop architecture where the first hop handles identity and the second hop, managed by Mullvad, handles encrypted traffic.
- The service utilizes the QUIC protocol to mimic HTTP/3 traffic, making it more resilient against deep packet inspection and internet censorship.
- Founder Carl Dong, a former Bitcoin Core contributor, emphasizes "trust minimization" by open-sourcing the client and supporting reproducible builds.
- The platform requires no email for registration and accepts anonymous payments via Monero and Bitcoin over the Lightning Network.
- Obscura operates as a small, independent team of six, avoiding venture capital influence to maintain a subscription-based business model.

### Why it Matters
This model challenges the traditional "no-logs" promise by ensuring that no single entity can correlate a user's identity with their browsing activity. By decentralizing trust, Obscura provides a technical alternative for users concerned about the risks of data breaches or legal subpoenas inherent in centralized VPN services.

articles.title: Community banks sue OCC over trust bank charters of crypto firms
articles.author: Cointelegraph by Michael Millard
articles.content:
Community banks sue OCC over trust bank charters of crypto firms
Community banking group’s lawsuit claims OCC has overstepped its mandate from Congress.
A community banks group sued a US bank regulator, claiming its decision to allow cryptocurrency companies to obtain limited national trust bank charters exceeds the authority Congress granted the agency.
The Independent Community Bankers of America (ICBA) filed the suit Friday in the US District Court for the District of Columbia.
The group claimed the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has granted cryptocurrency firms the credibility of a US bank charter without sufficient safeguards or compliance with normal bank requirements.
“The OCC’s decision to allow companies to obtain national trust bank charters to conduct substantial non-fiduciary activities exceeds the authority Congress granted the agency,” ICBA president and CEO Rebeca Romero Rainey said in a statement. “Congress did not create the national trust charter as a side door into the banking system for crypto firms seeking the credibility of a federal bank charter without the Community Reinvestment Act obligations, consolidated supervision, capital and liquidity standards, and FDIC insurance that apply to insured depository institutions.”
The ICBA is asking the court to return the OCC to its statutory limits, Rainey added.
The OCC was asked for comment on the lawsuit but had not replied by the time of publication.
Cointelegraph reported in August that under President Donald Trump and OCC head Jonathan Gould, the agency has approved or conditionally approved multiple applications from crypto companies seeking trust charters to expand their services in the US.
Still, the trust bank charters do not allow companies to accept deposits or make loans, distinguishing them from conventional commercial banks, Cointelegraph reported.
articles.summary:
The Independent Community Bankers of America has filed a lawsuit against the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, challenging its authority to grant national trust charters to cryptocurrency firms.

### Key Points
- The ICBA filed the lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia on Friday.
- The trade group alleges the OCC bypassed congressional intent by allowing crypto companies to obtain federal bank charters without meeting standard regulatory requirements.
- Plaintiffs argue these firms avoid obligations like the Community Reinvestment Act, FDIC insurance, and strict capital liquidity standards.
- The OCC began approving or conditionally approving these trust charters for crypto companies under the Trump administration.
- National trust charters currently restrict firms from accepting traditional deposits or issuing commercial loans.

### Why it Matters
This legal challenge highlights a growing tension between traditional financial institutions and the expanding regulatory footprint of digital asset companies. A court ruling could force federal regulators to tighten oversight of crypto firms or potentially revoke the legitimacy granted by these specialized banking charters.

articles.title: LinkedIn cofounder says AI infrastructure is the 'only reason we're not in a recession'
articles.author: Truman Dickerson,Madison Hoff
articles.content:
Many Americans are bristling over the data center buildout. Reid Hoffman says he's thankful for it.
The LinkedIn cofounder said so during an appearance on the "Newcomer" podcast that was released Friday. Hoffman credited the huge amount of capital behind the AI infrastructure buildout for being "the only reason we're not in a recession."
He said "most of that capital" doesn't go to the areas where data centers are being built.
"Most of that's more distributed across the country," he said. "That's great."
Hoffman said that in addition to powering the AI boom, data center construction also provides work for construction workers, electricians, carpenters, real estate agents, and lawyers.
"All of this capital infusion, people think, 'Oh, that's just going to the tech companies,'" he said, adding that a "massive percentage of it is going towards data center construction."
Data centers have recently emerged as a source of bipartisan fury as midterm elections approach. Both Republican and Democratic governors have recently moved to curtail or restrict construction.
In a poll released last week by the Pew Research Center, which surveyed people in August, half of rural Americans said data centers "are mostly bad for the environment" — a figure substantially higher than in January, when it sat at 32%.
At the same time, US investors have mind-boggling amounts of money riding on the hope that AI will soon become profitable. Data centers will play a key role in that.
And for AI companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, and others, the issue is existential. Without AI data centers, they can't power the products they sell. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has recently suggested that new data centers could be built far from where people live, such as in the desert.
For Hoffman, the issue is simple: Data center builders need to work fairly with local communities to ensure that both sides get a good deal, he said.
As for his recession statements, the US economy is still on solid ground, even outside the blistering pace of tech capital expenditures.
Despite a disappointing September jobs report, unemployment remained low, suggesting a middling rather than a recessionary labor market. And, overall, economic growth is still strong. Real gross domestic product grew at a 2.2% annual rate in the second quarter; that measure typically declines during recessions. Real personal income minus transfers, another recession indicator, is also up from a year ago, and consumer spending is still growing.
articles.summary:
LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman argues that massive capital investment in AI data center construction is a primary economic driver currently preventing a recession in the United States.

### Key Points
- Reid Hoffman stated on the "Newcomer" podcast that data center infrastructure spending supports diverse sectors, including construction, real estate, and legal services.
- A recent Pew Research Center poll shows that 50% of rural Americans now view data centers as environmentally harmful, up from 32% in January.
- Major tech firms including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google rely on these facilities to power their artificial intelligence products.
- OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has proposed building future data centers in remote desert locations to mitigate local community concerns.
- Despite public opposition and regulatory pushback from state governors, investors continue to pour significant capital into AI infrastructure to ensure future profitability.

### Why it Matters
The rapid expansion of data centers has become a contentious political issue as local communities weigh environmental concerns against the economic benefits of infrastructure investment. This tension highlights the broader challenge of scaling AI technology while balancing the existential needs of tech companies with public sentiment and regional development.

articles.title: This Harry Potter Edition Phone From Realme Is the Coolest Collab of 2026
articles.author: Prakhar Khanna
articles.content:
Realme is back with another special edition phone in collaboration with Warner Bros. After a color-changing Game of Thrones edition collectible, the company has launched a Harry Potter-themed phone. The Realme 16 Pro 5G Harry Potter Edition pairs themed exterior styling with the standard model’s core hardware and bundles it with a bunch of goodies.
I’m a Potterhead, and I couldn’t wait for my unit to arrive. As soon as it reached my doorstep, I unboxed it and went hands-on with the device. From the unboxing experience to its software, this is a Hogwarts makeover any Harry Potter fan would love.
Alohomora! Unboxing the Harry Potter phone
The new Realme special edition phone comes in a chest-shaped box that resembles Harry’s Hogwarts trunk. Unfortunately, casting the Alohomora spell doesn’t unlock it; you’ll need to use your thumbs, like any other Muggle. Once unlocked, the neat presentation screams of “You’re a wizard, Harry!” and pulls you into the world of Harry Potter.
More from CNET
On the left side, you’ll find a brown box carrying the phone case and a SIM-ejector tool, both of which carry the Harry Potter branding with the Hogwarts crest. Put your wand on the box (you don’t get one with the phone), incant “Accio,” and… yeah, it does nothing.
You need to pull out the case, which is in a matching brown color. And that’s when you start getting to a number of other fun goodies thrown in for Harry Potter fans.
Moving to the right side, there’s another rectangular cardboard holder with the Sorting Hat logo on top of it. Inside, you get the Hogwarts letter, Platform Nine and Three-Quarters train ticket, bookmarks of each house and four postcards.
The letter carries a wax-like stamp on the back, while the bookmarks come with a holder, where you can place your favorite house’s emblem. I added the Hufflepuff badge to it, and it’s now my favorite bookmark.
Move the rectangular holder out of the way and you’re greeted with the phone itself. But before reaching the device, I must tell you, Realme has also color-coded the charger and wire to match the theme. This is worth a mention because several phone collaborations limit the theme to the device and collectibles, leaving the phone accessories plain white. But that’s not the case here and I appreciate it.
A customized Harry Potter-styled phone
With a simple swish and flick, wizards and witches can use the Wingardium Leviosa spell and the phone levitates out of the box. However, Muggles will need to pick it up like any other device. The phone itself continues the theme with gold accents on the dark brown design. There are plenty of hidden Harry Potter references that are delightful to uncover.
Starting with the camera module, it has two prominent camera rings with a little golden diamond between them. Look closely, and you’ll find they resemble Hedwig’s eyes and nose. The camera module’s gold-colored deco looks great against the brown rear panel, which has a leather-like texture. It feels nice in the hand.
The rear panel also has a diamond pattern, which, according to Realme, is inspired by wizard’s chess from the books and movies. It imprints the four-house crest along with the “Draco Dormiens Nunquam Titillandus” motto and the Harry Potter and Realme logos, which are inscribed underneath.
Put it under the sun and you’ll see the crest light up in the house-specific colors. Realme calls it the Quadra Light-Sensing Color-changing Tech, which lights up specific areas when you shine a UV light over it. Also (I almost missed this), the right side of the phone has “Welcome to Hogwarts” engraved into it.
The references don’t end here. Realme’s Harry Potter-fication runs deeper. When you power on the phone, there’s a Harry Potter boot animation and a custom letter wax fingerprint animation.
Then you’re greeted with a Hogwarts-specific UI, with the castle on the wallpaper and more than 30 custom icons. For example, the Phone app is a red telephone booth, whereas the Notes app is a quill. Even the Google apps’ icons are customized to match the theme.
What about the specifications?
I haven’t used the Realme 16 Pro 5G Harry Potter Edition as my full-time phone yet, but it packs impressive specifications. You get a 6.78-inch AMOLED screen with a 1.5K resolution and a 144Hz refresh rate. It boasts up to 6,000 nits in peak brightness. While I haven’t tested it, the screen was easily legible under direct sunlight.
This special-edition Realme phone is powered by the MediaTek Dimensity 7300-Max chip, paired with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of onboard storage.
You get a 200-megapixel primary camera, accompanied by an 8-megapixel ultrawide-angle sensor with a 112-degree field of view. On the front is a 50-megapixel selfie shooter. To top it off, the phone packs a 7,000-mAh battery with support for 80-watt fast charging. It runs a customized version of Realme UI 7.0 based on Android 16. It is limited to 5,000 units and is priced at INR 62,999 (~$655) in India. Harry Potter fans in the US won’t be able to buy this one, but Google’s Pixel phones recently received Harry Potter theme packs that add their own magical customizations.
It is 2026. It’s only fair for Hogwarts to finally adopt smartphones in addition to using Floo Powder to communicate. The Realme 16 Pro 5G Harry Potter Edition feels quite special as a fan of the books and movies. It is evident that the two companies have put a lot of thought into this collaboration.
Realme effortlessly put me back into the realm of the Wizarding World. From the trunk case and its unboxing experience, down to the customized software, I loved every bit of it. Then came the hidden references and collectible items. I have a strong Harry Potter bias, but this is my favorite limited edition phone of all time. It is Riddikulus-ly cool.
articles.summary:
Realme has launched a limited-edition Harry Potter version of its 16 Pro 5G smartphone, featuring extensive thematic design elements, custom software, and exclusive collectibles for franchise fans.

### Key Points
- The device features a leather-like brown rear panel with gold accents, a Hogwarts crest, and light-sensing color-changing technology.
- Hardware includes a 6.78-inch 144Hz AMOLED display, MediaTek Dimensity 7300-Max processor, 12GB of RAM, and a 7,000-mAh battery.
- The phone is equipped with a 200-megapixel primary camera and supports 80-watt fast charging.
- Software customizations include a Harry Potter boot animation, themed icons, and a Hogwarts-inspired user interface.
- The package includes a trunk-shaped box, house-themed bookmarks, postcards, and a Hogwarts acceptance letter.
- Limited to 5,000 units, the device is priced at INR 62,999 and is currently exclusive to the Indian market.

### Why it Matters
This collaboration highlights the growing trend of using niche pop-culture branding to differentiate hardware in a saturated smartphone market. By integrating deep software and accessory customization, Realme aims to drive collector interest and brand loyalty among dedicated fan bases.

articles.title: Radical electric bikemaker is coming to the USA next year
articles.author: Utkarsh Sood
articles.content:
Very few people understand what it actually takes for a company to become a household name. With small-ticket products, the odds are at least somewhat kinder. Something sitting on a supermarket shelf can grab your attention, cost little enough to try on a whim, and, if you like it, be bought again and again. Familiarity builds quickly when the barrier to entry is a few dollars.
Motorcycles don't work that way. Nobody casually throws a few thousand dollars at a bike they've never heard of just because the badge looks interesting.
It's a big-ticket purchase, it's deeply personal, and for a lot of riders, the name on the tank carries almost as much weight as the machine itself. Building that kind of trust takes years, sometimes generations.
Take, for instance, some of the brands we now take for granted. Harley-Davidson didn't become synonymous with American motorcycling overnight. Indian Motorcycle has roots stretching back more than a century, despite disappearing and being resurrected along the way. Triumph Motorcycles has spent decades turning a once-fading British marque into a genuinely global name. And Royal Enfield, which is now one of the most recognizable brands on the planet, has had an even longer, stranger journey from its British beginnings to becoming an Indian motorcycle powerhouse.
That's the thing about becoming a household motorcycle name: there really isn't a shortcut.
And you'd think all the advancements in tech would have made that easier. There are more ways than ever to discover a new brand, more sophisticated motorcycles to build, more accessible manufacturing technology, and a global audience sitting just a click away. Getting attention is one thing. Convincing somebody to actually hand over their money, and then come back for another motorcycle years later, is considerably harder.
Which brings us to Ultraviolette. It isn’t a household name in the motorcycle market yet. It’s not a one-hit wonder, either. It might be lesser-known in Western circles, but where it’s from, the brand is carrying a lot of momentum with it. And maybe that’s why its imminent US arrival is getting people talking.
The company has spent the past few years building a reputation around electric motorcycles that are unapologetically performance-focused and technologically ambitious. All in a country that already produces a ton of motorcycles every year – most of which are affordable, small-bore city commuters.
But what separates Ultraviolette from a very populated two-wheeler segment in India is how unapologetically it has positioned itself as a technology and performance brand. Rather than trying to beat the likes of TVS, Royal Enfield, and Bajaj at their own game with yet another commuter, Ultraviolette has gone after the enthusiast with motorcycles that look, feel, and perform like they belong several rungs higher up the ladder.
And what’s even more impressive is that the company doesn’t rely on cheap white-labeled components to slap on its bikes and call it a day. There’s a heavy emphasis on in-house engineering, from its battery and powertrain technology to software, connected features, and radar-based safety systems.
And now, after expanding into 20 European countries and raising another US$85 million to scale production and develop its next generation of global EV platforms, Ultraviolette is setting its sights on an altogether bigger prize: America.
The company says it plans to enter the US market in 2027, potentially turning what started as an ambitious Indian electric-motorcycle startup into a genuinely global two-wheeler brand.
That new funding was led by Yali Capital and TDK Ventures. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan has also backed the company personally, with the veteran tech executive – who also serves as chairman of investment firm Walden International – joining Ultraviolette in an advisory role.
The fresh capital will help Ultraviolette ramp up manufacturing of its F77 and X-47 electric motorcycles, bring the Tesseract scooter and Shockwave electric enduro into production, and fund the development of its next generation of electric moto platforms.
We’ve been told that Ultraviolette is preparing for considerably greater production volumes for now, with the company having announced plans for a new manufacturing facility in India with an eventual capacity of up to 500,000 bikes a year.
Ultraviolette’s current lineup is as diverse as it can be for a moto brand that’s barely a decade old. At one end sits the F77, its performance-focused electric motorcycle and the model that put the company on the map.
On the other sits the newer X-47 that brings radar-assisted safety tech and an altogether more everyday-friendly approach to electric two-wheelers. Then there’s the Tesseract, which takes the scooter formula and crams it with an almost unreasonable amount of technology. And the most recent announcement that’s set to be released in the first quarter of 2027 is the Shockwave, an electric enduro aimed squarely at riders who'd rather spend their weekends throwing a bike at dirt than commuting through traffic.
Lurking above all of them is the F99, Ultraviolette’s seriously quick, fully faired electric superbike that serves as a rather unsubtle demonstration of what the company’s engineering department is capable of. Also dubbed "India’s first superbike."
For a company still finding its feet on the global stage, that’s a surprisingly broad spread. One that looks considerably more ambitious than most newfound moto brands.
But putting America on a presentation slide and actually establishing yourself in the US motorcycle market are two very different propositions. Of course, there’ll be homologation and regulatory hurdles, distribution and service quirks, parts availability and pricing details that will need some ironing out before all of that.
Added to all that, the US is home to some of the world's most established motorcycle brands, arguably the most influential enthusiast culture, and riders who have more choice than ever. If Ultraviolette can establish itself there, it won't merely have added another export market to its map.
It'll have taken a significant step toward becoming the thing every young motorcycle company ultimately wants to be: a name people know before they've even seen the motorcycle.
Source: Ultraviolette via Business Standard
articles.summary:
Indian electric motorcycle manufacturer Ultraviolette plans to enter the United States market by 2027, aiming to transition from a regional startup into a globally recognized performance brand.

### Key Points
- Ultraviolette secured $85 million in funding led by Yali Capital and TDK Ventures to scale production and develop new electric platforms.
- The company is building a new manufacturing facility in India with an eventual annual capacity of 500,000 motorcycles.
- Current product offerings include the performance-focused F77, the radar-equipped X-47, the Tesseract scooter, and the upcoming Shockwave electric enduro.
- The brand distinguishes itself through in-house engineering of battery technology, software, and safety systems rather than using white-labeled components.
- Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan has joined the company as an advisor to support its global expansion efforts.

### Why it Matters
Successfully entering the US market would validate Ultraviolette’s strategy of prioritizing high-end performance and proprietary technology over the mass-market commuter segment. Establishing a foothold in America represents a critical milestone for the company as it attempts to compete with legacy motorcycle manufacturers on a global scale.

articles.title: I filled my home with Amazon Echo devices, but these are the only ones I'd buy again
articles.author: Jonathon Jachura
articles.content:
My house has an Echo in almost every room. It started with a single Echo Dot. Over a few years, it grew into a small fleet of Dots, Echo Shows, and Echo Hubs tied to Ring sensors, myQ garage doors, Hue lights, and three thermostat zones. I've stuck with Alexa for reasons I've laid out before, mostly because it works with nearly everything I plug in.
Living with that many Echos taught me something the product pages never mention. Some of them do real work every day, while one type spends most of its life displaying the time. If I were starting over in an empty house, I'd skip that one and put the money toward more of the three below.
Echo Dot (5th gen)
The cheapest Echo in my house does the most work
An Echo Dot costs around $40, and it often drops lower during Prime sales. That price is why I was comfortable putting one in nearly every room. Voice control was the original reason I bought them. The temperature sensor Amazon added to the 5th-gen model is why I kept buying more.
My home runs three HVAC zones on Amazon Smart Thermostats, and a thermostat on a hallway wall only knows how warm the hallway is. Pairing Dots in the bedrooms, basement, and great room with those thermostats gives each zone readings from the rooms people actually occupy. I covered how that fixed a stubborn hot room with Echo's built-in temperature sensors. Each Dot also works as a room-level trigger for routines, so a command spoken in one room affects that room.
The weak spot is audio. Podcasts, timers, and weather updates sound fine, but music comes across thin. If you want fuller sound in a similar footprint, the newer Echo Dot Max (about $100) adds a second driver. I haven't used one myself.
Echo Hub
A wall-mounted control panel beats talking to a speaker
I own four Echo Hubs, and they changed how everyone else in my house uses the smart home. Voice commands work well for me because I remember what I named every light group. Guests and family members don't. The Hub gives them an 8-inch touchscreen with room-by-room controls, camera feeds, and device tiles, so turning off the patio lights no longer depends on guessing the right phrase.
It also doubles as a Zigbee, Thread, and Matter hub. That saved me from buying separate bridges for several sensors. Mounting matters more than most buyers expect. I powered two of mine over Ethernet, so a single cable inside the wall handles power and nothing dangles below the screen. If you already have network runs in your walls, the extra effort pays off.
The speaker is small, so don't count on it for music. Treat the Hub like a light switch with a screen, and at roughly $180, it's one of the best values Amazon sells.
Echo Show 15
A big screen in the kitchen justifies the price
I own two Echo Show 15s, and the one on my kitchen counter gets more use than any other Echo in the house. Its 15.6-inch display is readable from across the room, which is the entire point. Our shared calendar, the shopping list, and the Ring doorbell feed live on the home screen, so nobody needs to unlock a phone to check who's at the door or what's happening tonight.
Alexa+ made it better. The redesigned interface supports oversized widgets and separate layouts, and follow-up questions no longer require repeating the wake word. Built-in Fire TV lets me put on a show while I cook, too.
At about $300 for the current model, it isn't an impulse purchase. Put it in the room with the most foot traffic, then spend an evening setting it up properly. Most owners barely scratch the surface of what the Show's screen can do, and that setup time is what separates a family command center from an overpriced photo frame.
Smaller Echo Shows
Stuck between a Dot and a Hub
The third Show in my house is a smaller Echo Show 8, and it's the one I wouldn't buy again. It isn't a bad device. It simply has no job that my other Echos don't already handle better.
For voice commands, music, and timers, a Dot does the same work for less money. For touch controls, the Hub's interface is built entirely around the smart home, while the smaller Show's screen splits attention among sponsored content, recipes, and rotating suggestions. Mine ends up showing the time for most of the day. The camera adds another tradeoff. I don't make video calls on it, so the lens brings privacy concerns without a matching benefit, especially in a bedroom.
If you truly want a mid-size display, the 2025 Echo Show 8 and Echo Show 11 run on Amazon's newer AZ3 Pro chip and ship ready for Alexa+. For most rooms, though, a Dot saves you the difference.
Match each Echo to a job before you buy it
After years of adding Echos one room at a time, my buying rule is simple. Dots belong anywhere you want voice control and temperature data. Hubs go on the walls where people already reach for light switches. One large Show belongs in the kitchen or wherever your household gathers. Anything that doesn't fill one of those roles tends to become an expensive clock. Start with a single Dot, connect it to your thermostat and a routine or two, and expand from there once you see which rooms need more.
articles.summary:
Amazon’s Echo product lineup offers specialized devices for different smart home needs, with the Echo Dot, Echo Hub, and Echo Show 15 providing the most practical daily utility.

### Key Points
- The 5th-gen Echo Dot ($40) provides essential voice control and includes a built-in temperature sensor for optimizing HVAC zones.
- The Echo Hub ($180) features an 8-inch touchscreen and acts as a central controller for Zigbee, Thread, and Matter smart home devices.
- The Echo Show 15 ($300) serves as a large-format family command center for calendars, doorbell feeds, and streaming media in high-traffic areas.
- Smaller Echo Show models often lack a distinct purpose, frequently serving only as clocks rather than functional smart home interfaces.
- Proper placement and setup, such as wall-mounting the Echo Hub, significantly improve the usability of Amazon’s smart home ecosystem for all household members.

### Why it Matters
Selecting the right hardware for specific rooms prevents unnecessary spending on devices that offer redundant features or limited utility. By matching Echo devices to their intended roles, users can create a more responsive and intuitive smart home environment that benefits the entire household.

articles.title: 5 Android Phones That Had Variable Aperture Cameras Before The iPhone 18 Pro
articles.author: staff@bgr.com (José Adorno)
articles.content:
5 Android Phones That Had Variable Aperture Cameras Before The iPhone 18 Pro
Long before Apple released the iPhone 18 Pro with a variable aperture on the main camera, which we consider the best smartphone camera of 2026, other Android players walked this path before — and eventually exited it. The first was Samsung with the 2018 Galaxy S9 and S9+. Over the years, other companies followed, like Huawei with the Mate 50 Pro, Sony with the Xperia Pro-I, and Xiaomi with its 14 Ultra phone. Always focused on the premium segment — and eventually expanding to the mid-range – what these smartphone manufacturers tried to achieve was a way to differentiate themselves from the wave of phones with similar specs.
By combining the expertise of famous brands like Leica and Zeiss, these smartphone manufacturers could bring more customization to their offerings as, usually, smartphones use a fixed aperture to capture the most light across several conditions. With variable aperture, customers can select manually how much light they want the phone to absorb, which can impact depth of field and offer more creativity when taking photos.
Variable aperture cameras on phones can be great for group photos, where you can ensure that several subjects remain in focus. Photos can also look sharper, and photographers can play with different lighting conditions, object movement, and more. Still, most of these companies eventually decided to phase out the technology, saving the extra effort that they would rather put somewhere else. These are some Android phones that had variable aperture cameras before the iPhone.
Samsung Galaxy S9
Introduced in March 2018, the Galaxy S9 was the first smartphone with a variable aperture with a f1.5 and f.24 dual option. According to Samsung, this smartphone worked like the human eye, as it would adjust to different lighting conditions. Besides that, Samsung's camera would also capture up to 12 versions of the same photo to ensure the image would have great contrast, while reducing noise. This camera was also responsible for Super Slow-mo captures at 960 frames per second, automatic Motion Detection, and Samsung's AR Emoji, a response to Apple's popular Memojis that you could even set as your own wallpaper. All that was possible thanks to a rear 12MP camera and a 12MP telephoto lens, and an 8MP selfie camera.
The Samsung Galaxy S9 also marked a few other improvements over the previous generation, which only had one main camera. While Apple was moving forward with Face ID technology, Samsung had a fingerprint sensor in the back of the phone — just underneath the cameras — which could become convenient once you discovered where to place your finger, but would most times just keep your camera lenses smudged with a 'clean your lenses" notification before you could take any photo.
Samsung continued to offer a variable aperture with its subsequent releases, including the Galaxy S20 and the Galaxy Note 10. However, costs and complexity of the hardware made the company ditch the technology. While Galaxy S27 was rumored to bring the feature back, these remain the reasons why Samsung might never restore it back to its phones.
Sony Xperia Pro-I
In 2021, in partnership with ZEISS, Sony released the Xperia Pro-I smartphone. This device has been the only Sony phone with a variable aperture. With f/2.0 to f/4.0 aperture, the company promised "outstanding low light performance, high dynamic range, and beautiful bokeh." Sony also promoted this Xperia Pro-I phone as the first smartphone to record 4K video at 120fps. While the PRO-I didn't live up to the expectations of a second generation with variable aperture, Sony eventually switched to true continuous optical zoom with telephoto lenses moving the glass element between focal lengths like 85mm and 125mm.
The Sony Xperia Pro-I featured a 6.5-inch 4K HDR OLED display with 120Hz refresh rate. It had the Qualcomm Snapdragon 888 5G processor, 12GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage with up to 1TB of expandable storage via a microSDXC slot. Focused for photography enthusiasts, this phone featured a triple-camera system led by a 12MP 1.0-inch Exmor RS main sensor with variable aperture and 24mm Zeiss Tessar T optics. This phone also featured a 12MP telephoto lens with 2x optical zoom and a 12MP ultrawide lens. Sony also had a 3D iToF depth sensor to improve shots, in addition to an 8MP front-facing camera.
Even though Sony is currently absent from the U.S. market, it still sells smartphones in a few regions. Among its offerings, Sony has the Xperia 10 VIII, the Xperia 1 VII, and the Xperia 10 VII, tackling the mid-range phone segment.
Huawei Mate 50 Pro
Released in 2022, Huawei was another company to introduce variable aperture for its main camera. Called Ultra Aperture XMAGE Camera, Huawei Mate 50 Pro focused on a Professional mode that would give users 10 different aperture sizes to choose from. With a 50MP sensor, the company said the lens was able to absorb 24% more light than the previous model thanks to a ultra-large f/1.4 aperture and RYYB sensor. This sensor was also responsible for an improved Super Night Mode to give low-light ambient shots a new life.
This phone also featured a 64MP periscope telephoto lens with 3.5x optical zoom and a 13MP ultrawide lens. The selfie camera featured a 13MP camera with a 3D ToF sensor for 3D face unlock. The Huawei Mate 50 Pro had a 6.74-inch OLED display with 120Hz refresh rate, and it was powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8+ Gen 1 chipset with 8GB of RAM, and up to 512GB of storage.
Unlike Samsung, Huawei continued releasing smartphones with a variable aperture, which included the 2023 Huawei P60 Pro phones, the Huawei Pura 70 Pro lineup released in 2024, and more recently the Pura 80 Pro and 80 ultra in 2025. Even more interestingly, the company brought this technology to mid-range lineups with the Huawei Nova 13 Pro and Nova 14 Pro. They feature a 50MP RYYB sensor with an f/1.4 to f/4.0 aperture, which shows a unique case of a company that kept betting on this technology for its phones.
Xiaomi 13 Ultra
Xiaomi was probably one of the loudest companies about the variable aperture feature. First partnering with Leica, the company offered a dual-step mechanism with the Xiaomi 13 Ultra in 2023, and then improved the technology by 2024 in the 14 Ultra with a stepless 10-blade aperture. However, after two big years of focusing on this function, the company silently removed the variable aperture with the Xiaomi 15 Ultra and moved back to a fixed f/1.63 aperture.
Among the reasons, Xiaomi focused on solving the "telephoto gap" problem by offering a continuous mechanical optical zoom with the 17 Ultra option, adding advanced sensors with dynamic range technology that could handle highlights and extreme light contrast directly at the pixel level, and also due to the weight and thickness of previous models. By dropping the extra mechanical motor, the company was able to make the main module simpler, lighter, and less prone to mechanical wear over time.
While Xiaomi moved away from the technology, at the time it launched, the company really promoted a phone focused on photographers, with a quad rear camera system sporting a main 50MP 1.0-inch sensor, and three additional 50MP lenses for ultrawide, 3.2x optical zoom, and 5x optical periscope telephotos. The phone also featured a 32MP selfie camera to take sharp shots, and a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 processor with up to 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage.
Honor Magic6 Pro
In 2024, Honor became the latest smartphone maker (before Apple) to bet on variable aperture. With its all-new Magic6 Pro, Honor opted for a 50MP main camera with variable aperture between f/1.4 and f/2.0, promising "to capture fast-paced moments in exceptional clarity without compromising on details." The smartphone also featured a 180MP telephoto camera with 2.5x optical zoom, up to 100x digital zoom, and a 50MP ultra-wide lens.
Unlike Samsung's Galaxy S9, where the primary focus was the variable aperture, this Honor release was a lot more than that, with a big focus on AI. The company touted improvements with the MagicOS 8.0, its own version of Android with Magic Capsule and Magical Portal features. For example, the Magic Portal would understand messages and user behavior to streamline tasks — like recognizing an address on a message and direct users to Google Maps. Magic Capsule, on the other hand, users would get more informational and related options on the notifications banner at the top of the screen.
This phone also featured a 6.8-inch OLED display with 120Hz refresh rate, Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 processor paired with up to 6GB of RAM, 1TB of storage, and a 5,600 mAh silicon-carbon battery with 80W of wired charging. What's more interesting is that, so far, Honor continues to bet on variable aperture, as its latest Magic7 Pro model still features a physical two-step variable aperture.
articles.summary:
Before the iPhone 18 Pro introduced variable aperture technology, several Android manufacturers, including Samsung, Sony, Huawei, Xiaomi, and Honor, experimented with the feature to enhance mobile photography capabilities.

### Key Points
- Samsung pioneered the feature in 2018 with the Galaxy S9, offering a dual f/1.5 and f/2.4 aperture to mimic the human eye.
- Sony’s 2021 Xperia Pro-I utilized a Zeiss-partnered lens with an f/2.0 to f/4.0 aperture before shifting focus to continuous optical zoom.
- Huawei remains a consistent proponent of the technology, integrating variable aperture into both its flagship Pura series and mid-range Nova lineups.
- Xiaomi featured a 10-blade stepless aperture in the 14 Ultra but abandoned the hardware in the 15 Ultra to reduce device thickness and mechanical complexity.
- Honor’s Magic6 Pro and Magic7 Pro utilize a two-step variable aperture alongside AI-driven software features like Magic Portal.

### Why it Matters
Variable aperture technology allows smartphone users to manually control light intake and depth of field, offering creative flexibility typically reserved for professional cameras. While many manufacturers eventually phased out the hardware due to cost, weight, and mechanical wear, these early implementations paved the way for modern mobile photography standards.

articles.title: Muse Creates Detailed Profiles of All Your Friends and Family
articles.author: Lily Hay Newman, Matt Burgess
articles.content:
Welcome to Kernel Panic!, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
Meta’s new personal assistant, Muse, has become a viral hit, with millions downloading the AI agent, connecting it to bank accounts, messages, or health data, and allowing it to complete tasks for them. But as Muse takes off among consumers, data from inside the app is providing insight into how it organizes and presents information to users.
In recent days, multiple researchers have extracted Muse’s internal files and dumped the agent’s operating instructions, providing a glimpse of how the system was built and behaves. Meta has maintained that it intended for these files to be accessible in the interest of transparency, and they do provide insight into how Muse responds to prompts and questions about, for example, highly politicized or sensitive topics.
Independent AI safety and security researcher Karan Joshi was able to extract an extensive array of Muse instructions and system prompts by using the regular chat interface to essentially ask Muse to copy and share its own software files. Joshi then shared his findings with WIRED.
One of Muse’s instructions appears to be the ability for it to create “a page for every person in the user’s life.” This hourly process involves compiling data on family, partners, friends, colleagues, “collaborators,” and people you “follow,” the instructions say.
The general idea is that Muse can use its “memory” (aka structured text files) to collect information about your relationships and the important people in your life. It can then make suggestions, like giving pointers on how to improve particular relationships or, say, where to take a coffee-loving friend for breakfast. Of course, it’s not unusual for AI chatbots to track social information in general—people have been asking ChatGPT for relationship advice for years now. But it’s interesting to see how Muse is set up given Meta’s history and vast access to social network data.
“What it seemed like to me—from all these prompts, system skills data, and things that they’re feeding into Muse—is that they want to understand your relationships that you have with real people,” says Joshi. “They’re trying to know you like a friend, which is honestly pretty creepy.”
Muse’s documentation says that a page may start “sparse” and then be filled out over time, potentially including sections like Facts, History, The relationship, In common, Open threads, and Strengthening. Meta’s instructions say Muse should only use the “evidence” it has available, and that invented details are worse than an empty page.
“Where they live, what they do, the threads that recur (the apartment move, the shared savings goal),” the instructions say. They add, too, that the model could record the “dates that matter,” such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person’s history could include backstory like “the trip in March, the argument that got resolved, the milestone last week.”
The instructions also focus on recording relationship details such as “how close they are, what it is built on, how they act with each other, and what it seems to need right now.” The Strengthening section suggests ways a relationship could be improved, including, “A reason to call, a date worth remembering, something they said to circle back on, a way to be there for them that matters.”
“We are giving AI systems much more information about us than we are getting information from them,” says Carissa Véliz, an associate professor at Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI. “It’s not only what we explicitly tell them, but what they can infer from us—correctly or incorrectly, both concerning for different reasons—and what they can piece together from other sources of data.”
Muse is architected so each individual user has their own dedicated virtual machine, which stores user data and context. This VM is inaccessible to other agents and users can wipe memories or disconnect external services at any time. Meta says that Muse is also designed to seek human confirmation before completing actions like sending an email or making a purchase, and that it has an audit log where users can see all of the agent’s activity and future plans.
“For any agent to be useful and actually help you achieve your goals, it needs to have context about you and those you interact with,” Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told WIRED in a statement. “Muse gathers that based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share, which is how it remembers the person who sent you an invoice is in fact the plumber who you previously hired to complete work in your bathroom or which flowers your spouse said they liked best.”
It’s become common for AI assistants to incorporate some sort of memory feature designed to allow greater personalization in responses and activity. Miranda Bogen, the director of the Center for Democracy and Technology’s AI Governance Lab, says Muse appears to have more emphasis on relationships and personal contacts than rivals’ systems. In general, these tools tend to offer some transparency and editing capabilities, and Muse does as well. If anything, though, Bogen notes that agents and assistants encourage people to proactively share more data with them versus focusing on culling data.
“These [AI assistant] tools are actively soliciting users to plug their whole lives in—their emails, calendars, financial institutions, everything in order to be helpful assistance,” Bogen says. “That’s dramatically more information than people might have otherwise given to some of these companies. The breadth of access to information that these tools have will lead to a ballooning of what they know about users.
Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.
articles.summary:
Meta’s new AI assistant, Muse, is facing scrutiny after researchers extracted internal instructions revealing the tool actively catalogs detailed personal relationship data to provide proactive user suggestions.

### Key Points
- Security researcher Karan Joshi extracted Muse’s internal system prompts by requesting the AI to share its own operating files.
- The instructions reveal Muse creates dedicated profiles for people in a user's life, tracking milestones, shared history, and relationship dynamics.
- Meta states the AI uses this data to offer personalized assistance, such as remembering birthdays or suggesting ways to strengthen specific social connections.
- Muse operates within individual virtual machines, allowing users to wipe stored memories or disconnect external services like bank accounts and email.
- Privacy experts warn that the tool’s design encourages users to share vast amounts of sensitive personal information, significantly expanding corporate data collection.

### Why it Matters
The development of Muse highlights a growing trend where AI assistants are designed to act as comprehensive personal repositories rather than simple task-oriented tools. This shift raises significant privacy concerns regarding how much intimate social and behavioral data users are willing to entrust to large technology companies.

articles.title: Best Crypto to Buy Before the Next Crash: Top 5 Coins to Watch Through the End of 2026
articles.author: Yuri Molchan
articles.content:
Crypto markets enter the final quarter of 2026 with stronger prices but rising macroeconomic pressure. Bitcoin has rebounded sharply since July, while Treasury yields have climbed to multi-decade highs.
That combination makes liquidity, adoption, and downside resilience increasingly important when building a Q4 watchlist.
Related: Best Altcoins to Buy in October 2026 Before the Next Crypto Rally
Why a Crypto Crash Risk Is Back on the Radar in Q4 2026
Crypto has recovered strongly, but several conditions now resemble periods that previously produced sharp corrections. Higher rates, stretched valuations, and changing ETF flows could quickly weaken risk appetite.
Bitcoin Has Rallied More Than 40% Since July
Bitcoin gained more than 40% during the third quarter as investors returned after the summer decline. The recovery pushed BTC▲$77,666.00 back above $80,000 entering October.
Strong rallies can attract momentum buyers, yet they also increase sensitivity to disappointing macroeconomic data. Profit-taking becomes another risk after rapid advances.
Rising Treasury Yields Are Creating New Pressure on Crypto
The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield recently moved above 5%, reaching levels unseen for decades. Higher yields increase the attractiveness of lower-risk dollar assets.
Crypto receives no guaranteed cash flow, making expensive money particularly important for valuations. Another surge in yields could pressure Bitcoin and altcoins simultaneously.
Are ETF Inflows Strong Enough to Support the Market?
Bitcoin ETF flows have improved after periods of significant withdrawals earlier in 2026. Renewed institutional demand has helped restore confidence around BTC.
However, flows can reverse quickly during risk-off periods. Sustainable support requires consistent allocations rather than several isolated days of strong inflows.
What Could Trigger the Next Crypto Sell-Off?
Another Federal Reserve hike could become an immediate catalyst. Rising oil prices and persistent inflation would increase that risk.
ETF outflows, geopolitical escalation, or weakening global equities could add pressure. Crypto-specific failures could make any broader decline substantially worse.
5 Best Crypto Coins to Watch Before a Crash
This watchlist focuses on assets with established liquidity, measurable adoption, institutional exposure, and identifiable catalysts. Downside risk also matters because every cryptocurrency remains volatile.
Liquidity and Market Capitalization
Deep liquidity matters during market stress because traders need reliable markets when volatility accelerates. Larger assets generally provide stronger exchange depth.
Bitcoin and Ethereum dominate this category. Solana also offers substantial liquidity, while LINK▼$11.38 and AAVE▼$125.97 remain smaller and more volatile.
Institutional Demand and ETF Flows
Institutional products can create persistent demand beyond retail speculation. Bitcoin and Ethereum currently benefit most directly from regulated investment vehicles.
Solana has also attracted growing institutional attention. Chainlink and Aave gain exposure differently through infrastructure, tokenization, and decentralized finance.
Network Activity and Real-World Adoption
Useful networks have demand beyond token trading. Ethereum dominates stablecoins and tokenized finance, while Solana supports high-throughput consumer applications.
Chainlink connects blockchains with external systems. Aave provides lending infrastructure, while Bitcoin remains primarily a monetary and settlement asset.
Upcoming Catalysts Through the End of 2026
Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade represents a major Q4 technical catalyst. Solana continues deploying its Alpenglow consensus overhaul.
Chainlink recently launched CCIP 2.0, while Aave V4 continues expanding. Bitcoin remains driven mainly by macro conditions and institutional demand.
Read more: Best Crypto to Invest in: Bitcoin, Ethereum or XRP? What the Latest ETF Flows Reveal
Downside Risk and Historical Drawdowns
Large altcoins can lose significantly more than Bitcoin during severe market corrections. Smaller DeFi tokens can experience even deeper drawdowns.
Historical performance does not guarantee future behavior. Still, liquidity and market structure provide useful clues about relative crash sensitivity.
1. Bitcoin (BTC): The Crypto Market’s Main Defensive Asset
Bitcoin remains the largest and most liquid cryptocurrency. That position often makes BTC the first crypto asset institutions return to after market stress.
Why Bitcoin Could Hold Up Better in a Market Crash
Bitcoin usually carries lower liquidity risk than smaller cryptocurrencies. Its global exchange depth can help absorb larger transactions during volatile periods.
Institutional access also differentiates BTC from most altcoins. Investors can gain exposure through established spot ETFs without directly holding cryptocurrency.
Bitcoin ETF Flows Are Back in Positive Territory
Spot Bitcoin ETFs have recently returned to net inflows after weaker periods earlier in 2026. That recovery supports the institutional demand narrative.
Citi also raised its Bitcoin outlook as ETF activity improved. Nevertheless, daily flows remain volatile and require continued monitoring.
What Could Drive Bitcoin Through the End of 2026
ETF demand could become the main positive catalyst if institutional allocations continue rising. Improving inflation data would provide additional support.
A pause in Federal Reserve tightening could also benefit BTC. Conversely, higher yields would make another sustained rally harder.
The Biggest Risks for BTC in a Crypto Sell-Off
Bitcoin remains vulnerable to forced liquidations despite its size. Leveraged futures positions can amplify relatively modest spot-market declines.
Another ETF reversal would remove an important source of demand. A broader global risk-off event could also overwhelm crypto-specific positive catalysts.
2. Ethereum (ETH): The Institutional Blockchain Play
Ethereum combines established DeFi infrastructure with a growing role in stablecoins and tokenized financial assets. Its Q4 roadmap adds another potential catalyst.
Why Ethereum Remains Central to Stablecoins and Tokenization
Ethereum continues hosting major stablecoins, lending protocols, decentralized exchanges, and tokenized assets. Layer-2 networks extend that ecosystem without replacing Ethereum settlement.
Institutional tokenization projects frequently use Ethereum-compatible infrastructure. This creates demand connected with financial applications rather than memecoin speculation alone.
Ethereum’s Glamsterdam Upgrade and the Q4 Catalyst
Glamsterdam remains scheduled for Q4 2026, although its final mainnet date has not been confirmed. Testing continues across Ethereum development networks.
The upgrade focuses on Layer-1 scaling and changes to transaction processing. Successful deployment could improve Ethereum’s long-term capacity.
Institutional ETH Demand Is Picking Up
Institutional interest in Ethereum has improved alongside the wider crypto recovery. ETF flows provide investors with another regulated route into ETH▲$2,518.27.
Tokenization also strengthens Ethereum’s institutional relevance. Financial companies increasingly experiment with funds, securities, and settlement systems using blockchain infrastructure.
What Could Send ETH Lower in the Next Crash
Ethereum usually experiences larger percentage declines than Bitcoin during aggressive risk-off periods. Weak DeFi activity could increase that downside.
ETF withdrawals would add another source of pressure. Delays or technical problems around major upgrades could also weaken sentiment.
3. Solana (SOL): High Growth With Higher Crash Risk
Solana offers strong network growth and high transaction capacity, but SOL▲$101.41 behaves like a higher-beta crypto asset. That creates greater upside and downside sensitivity.
Why Solana’s Network Activity Matters
Solana supports decentralized exchanges, payments, memecoins, tokenized assets, and consumer-focused applications. High activity demonstrates continued demand for blockspace.
Network usage matters because speculative interest alone cannot sustain an ecosystem indefinitely. Persistent transaction demand provides a stronger foundation.
Solana ETF Flows and Institutional Interest
Institutional interest in Solana has expanded as regulated products broaden beyond Bitcoin and Ethereum. That provides SOL with another potential demand channel.
ETF-related demand remains smaller than Bitcoin’s institutional market. Therefore, Solana remains more sensitive to changes in speculative positioning.
What the Alpenglow Upgrade Could Mean for SOL
Alpenglow represents a major redesign of Solana’s consensus system. Its target is roughly 150-millisecond finality, compared with considerably slower finality previously.
The rollout focuses first on the Votor voting protocol. Faster finality could improve settlement speed for payments, trading, and financial applications.
Why SOL Could Fall Harder Than Bitcoin in a Sell-Off
SOL historically behaves as a higher-beta cryptocurrency. Traders often reduce exposure to such assets faster when market conditions deteriorate.
Its smaller market capitalization also increases volatility compared with Bitcoin. Leveraged trading can intensify those movements during rapid declines.
Related: Best Arc Memecoins in 2026: Early Arc Chain Tokens to Watch Before They Take Off
4. Chainlink (LINK): The Infrastructure Bet for the Next Crypto Cycle
Chainlink provides data, interoperability, and connectivity infrastructure across multiple blockchains. That gives LINK exposure to broader onchain financial development.
Why Chainlink Is Becoming Critical to Tokenized Finance
Tokenized assets need reliable pricing, reserve data, identity controls, and cross-chain communication. Chainlink provides infrastructure for several of those functions.
Its role differs from Layer-1 networks competing for users. Chainlink instead connects applications, assets, blockchains, and traditional financial systems.
Chainlink’s Banking and Payments Integrations
Chainlink has expanded work with financial institutions, payment infrastructure, and blockchain networks. Its technology has also featured in projects involving SWIFT.
Such integrations matter because institutional tokenization requires connectivity between existing systems and public or private blockchains. Chainlink targets that interoperability layer.
How CCIP Could Benefit LINK Through the End of 2026
CCIP allows tokens, messages, and data to move across supported blockchain networks. The recently launched CCIP 2.0 adds institutional controls and compliance functionality.
Greater adoption could strengthen Chainlink’s strategic position in multichain finance. However, protocol usage does not automatically translate directly into LINK price appreciation.
The Biggest Risks to the Chainlink Investment Case
LINK remains an altcoin and can suffer large losses during market-wide deleveraging. Infrastructure adoption may also develop slower than investors expect.
Competition represents another risk. Blockchain projects can build alternative interoperability solutions or use competing providers for specific services.
5. Aave (AAVE): The DeFi Blue Chip to Watch
Aave remains one of the established decentralized lending protocols. Aave V4 creates a new growth story but also introduces additional execution risk.
Why Aave V4 Changes the Investment Case
Aave V4 redesigns important components of the protocol around liquidity, risk management, and market deployment. The system aims to improve capital efficiency.
Expansion across additional networks could increase addressable demand. Its modular architecture also supports more specialized lending markets.
Aave V4 Surpasses $1 Billion in Deposits
Aave V4 surpassed $1 billion in deposits during September 2026. Active loans reached approximately $310 million as adoption continued expanding.
The milestone provides evidence of real capital moving into the new architecture. Deposits alone, however, do not guarantee sustainable protocol revenue.
How Tokenized Assets Could Expand Aave’s Market
Aave can potentially connect DeFi lending with tokenized real-world assets. Its Base deployment already supports a market involving tokenized equities as collateral.
That development widens lending beyond traditional crypto collateral. Continued tokenization could therefore expand the range of assets available within DeFi.
What Could Happen to AAVE During a DeFi Sell-Off
AAVE could experience substantial volatility during a severe DeFi downturn. Falling collateral prices often increase liquidations and reduce investor risk appetite.
Smart-contract concerns could intensify selling further. Smaller market capitalization also gives AAVE greater downside sensitivity than Bitcoin or Ethereum.
Bitcoin vs. Ethereum vs. Solana vs. Chainlink vs. Aave
These five cryptocurrencies represent different parts of the market. Bitcoin emphasizes monetary liquidity, while the others provide programmable blockchain infrastructure.
Which Coins Have the Strongest Liquidity?
Bitcoin and Ethereum offer the deepest overall markets among these five assets. SOL follows with substantial exchange liquidity and derivatives activity. LINK remains highly tradable but smaller. AAVE has the narrowest liquidity profile within this watchlist.
Which Projects Have the Strongest Institutional Adoption?
Bitcoin has the clearest institutional investment channel through large spot ETFs. Ethereum combines ETF access with tokenization and stablecoin infrastructure.

articles.title: US court halts AI nude-image ban challenged by Musk
articles.author: RT
articles.content:
US court halts AI nude-image ban challenged by Musk
A US appeals court has blocked Minnesota’s ban on AI-generated fake nude images, handing Elon Musk’s xAI an early victory in its free-speech challenge to the law.
The state’s anti-nudification legislation – the first in the nation – which took effect last month, targets apps and websites that enable non-consensual sexualized deepfakes, with fines of up to $500,000 per image. It was spearheaded by state Senator Erin Maye Quade after a man allegedly used social media photos to create explicit images of more than 80 women without their consent. Quade likened the measure to longstanding laws against peeping through windows to take photographs.
Musk’s xAI challenged the law in July on First Amendment grounds, calling it an “overbroad, content-based ban on free speech” and warning that penalties could run into the billions of dollars.
This comes as the company faces allegations involving the content the law targets. A class-action lawsuit proposed earlier this year claims that xAI’s Grok Imagine was used to create and distribute child sexual abuse material from real images, and accuses xAI of failing to provide the authorities with information on users who allegedly ‘nudified’ them.
A lower court rejected xAI’s bid to stop the Minnesota law last month. On Friday, however, the St. Louis-based 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals granted an injunction, putting the legislation on hold while the legal challenge continues.
Minnesota urged the court to keep the law in place, arguing that it is needed to combat the “staggering amount” of child sexual abuse material generated by AI products such as Grok Imagine. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison’s office said it is disappointed by the ruling and will continue defending the law.
XAI previously mounted a similar First Amendment challenge to a California law restricting AI-generated election deepfakes. A federal judge struck it down last year, finding the restrictions, as written, amounted to unconstitutional censorship. XAI also argues that Grok Imagine has “rigorous protections” against illegal content and has begun suing users it accuses of bypassing safeguards to create non-consensual sexual images.
XAI’s Grok earlier faced scrutiny outside the US after users flagged instances of the chatbot being used to alter photos of women into sexualized images without their consent, as well as cases involving minors. The reports prompted investigations and warnings in the EU, India, France, and the UK. Indonesia and Malaysia temporarily restricted access to Grok. X subsequently tightened safeguards around its image-generation and editing tools.
Losing control of AI?
The news comes amid broader unease over rapidly advancing AI, from privacy and copyright risks to threats to the livelihoods of human creators, with copyright disputes already sparking dozens of lawsuits.
Recently, attention has shifted to increasingly autonomous models going rogue and acting outside their intended environments. Since ChatGPT creator OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and accessed Hugging Face servers over the summer, models from companies such as Google, Anthropic, and Meta have gained unauthorized access to or attempted to breach systems belonging to businesses, governments, and international organizations.
Just this week, AI research company Transluce said AI agents tried to hack a Canadian government website, although Ottawa did not report a breach. Asymmetric Security separately found OpenAI models accessed data from 55 websites, including those of the CDC, SEC, and International Energy Agency, using tactics such as erasing records that made their activity harder to detect.
AI companies have begun reporting rogue behavior by their models with growing frequency. OpenAI said on Wednesday that its models may have bypassed safeguards or negatively affected systems at more than 100 organizations, significantly expanding the known scale of incidents. Though AI companies say the the breaches have so far caused little or no harm, they have raised questions over whether developers can maintain control as models gain greater autonomy. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently called for a “balanced rate” of development to give safeguards time to catch up – an appeal backed by Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
US President Donald Trump has rejected the idea of slowing AI development, dismissing fears of AI going rogue as “a hoax.” Amid mounting concerns, however, he and executives from six leading AI companies signed a voluntary White House accord on Tuesday pledging stronger safeguards, including measures to prevent models from hacking or accessing systems in unintended ways.
